strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing manual initialization for 6D pose estimation and recovering from tracking failures under occlusion, viewpoint changes, and rapid motion.
The proposed system is pragmatically motivated and combines segmentation, rendered 3D references, feature matching, pose registration, and re-localization into a coherent pipeline.
The evaluation includes several standard 6D pose/segmentation datasets such as LM-O, YCB-Video, T-LESS, TUD-L, and HB, and reports both accuracy and runtime.

The paper includes useful ablations for language injection, number of HSFA layers, DINOv2 fine-tuning, and the TOM attention classifier, which helps identify which components contribute to the reported gains.
weaknesses: The central annotation-free/self-supervised claim is not well supported. The method optimizes pixel-level losses against target masks, the appendix describes augmenting query images with corresponding masks, and the tracking dataset is built using BOP ground-truth masks. This conflicts with repeated claims that training uses only unlabeled RGB frames and no manual annotations.

The comparison protocol is unclear and potentially unfair. SOM is trained on BOP datasets and evaluated on BOP test sets, then compared against supervised, unsupervised, and leaderboard methods under a new 'self-supervised' category whose supervision assumptions are not rigorously matched. It is also unclear whether object instances or dataset-specific priors overlap in ways that weaken the zero-shot/generalization claims.

The pose-estimation evaluation is too narrow for the paper's state-of-the-art claims. Table 1 compares mainly against CNOS+FoundationPose and a ground-truth-mask upper bound on two datasets; it omits stronger direct pose-estimation baselines and standard BOP pose leaderboard comparisons. The claim of SOTA annotation-free 6D pose estimation is therefore not established.

The tracking evaluation relies on synthetically modified YCB-Video sequences with random frame dropping and random masks. This is useful as a stress test but does not convincingly demonstrate robustness to real physical occlusion, motion blur, camera motion, or re-entry in deployment. The custom tracking dataset is only briefly described and not sufficiently validated.

Runtime claims are incomplete. The paper reports component-level times, but not a full end-to-end latency including rendering, language prompt generation, CLIP/DINO feature extraction, SAM/FastSAM/SAM2 prompting, FoundationPose registration/tracking, and re-registration. The reported 0.183 s per segmentation image and 98 ms tracking time also make the 'real-time' claim ambiguous.

Methodological details are inconsistent across the main text and appendix. The optimizer is described as AdamW in the setup, SGD in Appendix D for SOM, and Adam for TOM; TOM training is reported as 15 epochs in the main text but 10 epochs in the appendix; the main loss uses Tversky+Focal while the appendix lists Focal, Dice, IoU, and Tversky with different weights and hyperparameters. These inconsistencies undermine reproducibility.

Several architectural details needed to reproduce HSFA and TOM are missing or underspecified, including tensor dimensions, exact DINO/CLIP variants, attention block configuration, prompt extraction from feature maps, thresholding for tracking failure, memory-pool update policy, and full segmentation model settings.

The presentation has many grammatical errors, formatting issues, and imprecise statements. Some figures are hard to read, and the paper sometimes overstates results, for example saying STORM matches ground-truth performance or exceeds supervised baselines without carefully qualifying the setting.

The paper does not provide a meaningful limitations or ethics discussion. For a robotics/perception system intended for deployment, it should discuss failure modes, safety implications of wrong pose estimates, dataset bias, reliance on proprietary or large pretrained models, and risks when tracking recovery fails.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing manual first-frame mask requirements for 6D pose estimation and recovering from tracking failures under occlusion or rapid motion.

The proposed system is modular and pragmatic, combining rendered 3D-model views, DINOv2/CLIP-style features, SAM/FastSAM segmentation, FoundationPose registration, and a learned failure detector. This is a potentially useful engineering direction.

The experiments cover several standard 6D pose/segmentation datasets, and the paper reports ablations for language injection, HSFA depth, DINO fine-tuning, and the attention-based tracking classifier.

The tracking-failure framing is a reasonable idea, and Table 4 suggests that learned attention-based matching can substantially improve over simple cosine similarity on the constructed classification task.
weaknesses: The central annotation-free/self-supervised claim is not convincingly supported. The main text says SOM is trained without manual annotations, but the appendix describes augmenting each query image with its corresponding mask, and the TOM dataset is explicitly built from BOP ground-truth masks. It is unclear what supervision is actually used, which directly undermines the main contribution.

Experimental methodology is underspecified and internally inconsistent. The paper gives conflicting details for losses and hyperparameters: the main method says Tversky plus focal loss with one set of weights, while the appendix lists focal, Dice, IoU, and Tversky losses with different parameters. Optimizer and training epoch descriptions also conflict between the main text and appendix.

The comparisons do not fully justify the state-of-the-art claims. The pose-estimation evaluation is limited mainly to FP+CNOS and FP+ground-truth-mask baselines on LM-O/YCB-V; the claimed DINO baseline is described but not clearly reported. The segmentation table mixes supervised, unsupervised, and the authors' self-supervised setting without enough protocol detail to ensure comparability.

The tracking evaluation is not sufficiently realistic. Failure cases are simulated by dropping frames and applying random masks, and the classifier is trained/evaluated on synthetic pair constructions. This does not establish robust recovery under real deployment conditions, nor does it separate failure detection quality from the downstream re-registration/pose pipeline.

The real-time claim is weak. Reported SOM inference is 0.183 s per image, and TOM tracking is about 98 ms; it is unclear whether these timings include rendering, LLM description generation, SAM/SAM2, FoundationPose registration, or re-registration. On high-end GPUs, the complete system may not meet typical real-time requirements.

Reproducibility is poor. The code field in the abstract appears blank, the custom/in-house tracking dataset is only described at a high level, implementation details are incomplete for rendering, prompting, memory-pool thresholds, re-registration triggers, model sizes, and evaluation scripts, and no released artifacts are actually provided in the manuscript.

Presentation quality is below ICML standards. There are many typos and formatting issues, malformed figure/table text, inconsistent naming such as SOM/TOM versus model/module, and several imprecise claims such as 'exceed state SOTA performances.' These issues make the technical content harder to trust.

Limitations and ethics are not adequately treated. The conclusion briefly mentions future work, but the paper does not seriously discuss failure modes, dependence on high-quality textured 3D models, domain shift from renders to real scenes, safety implications for robotics, or risks from false recovery after tracking loss.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck in 6D pose estimation: removing first-frame manual masks and recovering after tracking failures. A system that combines automatic segmentation, pose registration/tracking, and re-localization from only a 3D model would be useful for robotics deployment.

The empirical results are promising. STORM improves over CNOS + FoundationPose on LM-O and YCB-Video pose metrics, gives strong segmentation mAP across several BOP datasets, and the tracking-loss detector substantially improves robustness on the modified YCB-Video setting with modest reported latency overhead.

The system design is sensible and well-motivated: multi-view rendering of the CAD model, DINO-style feature matching, SAM/SAM2 prompting, FoundationPose registration/tracking, and a learned failure detector form a plausible pipeline. The ablations on language injection, HSFA depth, and attention in TOM help support some component-level design choices.

The appendices include useful metric definitions, augmentation settings, hardware, optimizer details, and construction of the tracking-pair dataset, which helps readers understand the intended experimental protocol.
weaknesses: The central annotation-free/self-supervised claim is not fully supported and is internally inconsistent. The main text says SOM is trained without manual annotations, but the appendix describes training each query image with a corresponding mask and optimizing segmentation losses. TOM also uses ground-truth BOP masks to construct memory crops and positive/negative pairs. This needs a much clearer distinction between rendered/synthetic masks, ground-truth masks, and human annotations.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient for a main-track systems paper. The abstract has a blank code link, the custom in-house TOM dataset is only promised to be released, and key implementation choices are ambiguous or contradictory. For example, the setup says AdamW and 15 TOM epochs, while the appendix says SGD for SOM, Adam for TOM, and 10 TOM epochs; the main loss is Tversky + focal, while the appendix lists focal, dice, IoU, and Tversky with different weights.

The evaluation has comparability concerns. Table 2 mixes supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised methods from the BOP leaderboard, but it is not sufficiently clear that all methods use the same inputs, training data, test protocol, and runtime hardware. The claim of surpassing supervised state of the art is therefore stronger than the evidence justifies.

The tracking evaluation is limited. Robustness is tested on a modified YCB-Video setting with synthetic frame dropping and random masks, but there is little analysis on real long-horizon tracking failures, object disappearance/re-entry, false re-registration, or multi-object identity switches. Since re-localization is a main contribution, this evaluation should be broader and more realistic.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Much of the pipeline is an integration of strong pretrained components and FoundationPose, with HSFA and the failure classifier as the main new pieces. The paper would be stronger if it isolated how much gain comes from the proposed attention modules versus better prompting, rendering, SAM variants, or engineering choices.

Presentation needs tightening. There are spelling/grammar issues, some figures/tables are hard to parse in the appendix, and several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially 'state-of-the-art', 'self-supervised', and 'annotation-free'. Limitations and ethics/broader impact are essentially absent; the conclusion lists future work but does not discuss failure modes, safety risks in robotic deployment, or dataset/model biases.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem for deployable robotic perception: reference-conditioned 6D pose tracking with automatic failure detection and re-localization. The motivation is clear, and the decomposition into segmentation, pose registration/tracking, and tracking-loss verification is practically meaningful.

The system-level design is promising. Hierarchical reference-query fusion for segmentation and a learned compatibility verifier for tracking drift are sensible components, and the paper makes a useful distinction between steady-state tracking costs and initialization/recovery costs.

The empirical scope is fairly broad for segmentation and pose evaluation, covering LM-O, YCB-Video, and several BOP datasets. Reporting comparisons against CNOS, FoundationPose with ground-truth masks, and BOP leaderboard methods helps position the method against relevant baselines.

The manuscript includes several useful ablations and implementation details, including HSFA depth, language conditioning, reference count, DINO fine-tuning, runtime profiling, and TOM matching variants. The limitations section is more honest than many submissions, especially in clarifying that the zero-shot claim is not category-disjoint generalization.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper repeatedly presents STORM as annotation-free and not relying on curated CAD models, but the training uses BOP object models/rendered references where available, the SAM3D alignment evaluation explicitly uses benchmark CAD models to align reconstructed meshes, and the benchmark object identities overlap between training and testing. This substantially weakens the claimed deployment setting.

The evaluation has fairness and protocol ambiguities. For Table 2, STORM is trained on BOP training splits including the evaluated datasets and auxiliary segmentation data, while many baselines have different supervision and runtime assumptions. It is unclear whether all methods are evaluated under exactly the same reference inputs, target protocol, postprocessing, and object identity exposure. The comparison to supervised and leaderboard methods therefore does not by itself establish a new state of the art.

The tracking-recovery results are underdeveloped. The stress test uses synthetic frame dropping and artificial rectangular occlusions on YCB-Video with mild perturbation probability, and the verifier is trained on synthetic compatible/incompatible crop pairs. This is useful as a diagnostic but does not convincingly demonstrate robust recovery under real tracking failures, severe occlusion, or robotic deployment conditions.

Several numerical and narrative inconsistencies reduce confidence. For example, the text says STORM on YCB-Video matches the ground-truth-mask setup exactly, but Table 1 shows lower ADD, ADD-S, and AR. Table 3 uses CAD-based alignment for SAM3D while the surrounding claims emphasize no CAD dependence. Some ablation AP values in the appendix use a scale/protocol that is not clearly connected to the main BOP AP results.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript has a blank code-availability line, relies on several large or recent frozen components, and does not provide enough detail to reproduce all preprocessing, BOP evaluation scripts, reference construction, SAM3D alignment choices, FoundationPose settings, threshold calibration splits, and random-seed handling. API/model-version dependence for VLM descriptors is also not fully specified.

The novelty is moderate. The system combines strong existing foundation components with attention-based fusion and a BCE-trained verifier; these are reasonable engineering choices, but the paper does not provide a particularly new learning principle or a deep analysis of why the proposed fusion/verifier should generalize beyond the tested pipeline.

The ethics/impact discussion is too cursory for a robotics perception system. It states no foreseeable negative societal consequences, but should discuss deployment risks from false pose estimates, failure-detector misses, overreliance in safety-critical manipulation, and dataset/model bias in industrial or household settings.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reference-conditioned 6D pose tracking with failure detection and re-localization, which is relevant for embodied AI and robotics deployments.
The overall system decomposition is sensible: a segmentation/front-end module, downstream FoundationPose tracking, and an explicit compatibility verifier for detecting drift.

The manuscript includes several useful ablations and implementation details, including reference-count/language conditioning, HSFA depth, TOM attention depth, latency profiling, and a limitations section that clarifies the zero-shot claim is not category-disjoint generalization.
weaknesses: The central claims are not adequately supported. The paper repeatedly claims annotation-free, CAD-free, single-image pose tracking, but the experiments train on BOP object identities, use rendered references from available 3D models during training, and align SAM3D reconstructions to benchmark CAD models for evaluation. This makes the practical CAD-free deployment claim much weaker than advertised.

The evaluation is not convincing enough for the stated contribution. The tracking benchmark is a mild synthetic stress test on YCB-Video with only 0.1 frame-drop and occlusion probability, and the main comparison is essentially STORM versus FoundationPose tracking without failure recovery. There are no strong tracking-recovery baselines, no real severe occlusion benchmark, and no analysis of false relocalizations in realistic sequences.

The segmentation comparison appears potentially unfair or at least under-specified. STORM is trained on BOP training splits including the same benchmark object identities, while many baselines have different supervision assumptions and leaderboard protocols. The paper claims state of the art from a 67.7 mean AP, but the exact evaluation protocol, target generation, reference source, and comparability to public BOP numbers are insufficiently documented.

The SAM3D experiment is circular for the CAD-free claim: the strong SAM3D result depends on CAD-based similarity alignment to the benchmark model. The paper states this is only for coordinate convention, but does not demonstrate that pose registration works comparably without curated CAD alignment in an actual deployment setting.

Methodological novelty is limited. HSFA is a fairly standard combination of self-attention, cross-attention, and FiLM/AdaLN-style language conditioning; TOM is a BCE-trained binary verifier with temporal smoothing. These are reasonable engineering choices, but the paper oversells them as a principled new framework without enough evidence that the specific proposed mechanisms, rather than pretrained DINO/SAM3D/FoundationPose components, drive the gains.

Reproducibility is weak. The code link is blank, several key components are frozen external foundation models that may be unavailable or version-sensitive, architecture details are incomplete, and the TOM validation/test split construction is not described precisely enough to rule out leakage from the same datasets/sequences used in evaluation.

The paper contains presentation and consistency problems. Some figures/text have formatting artifacts, the HSFA ablation reports AP around 94-95% while the main BOP AP is around 68% without clearly explaining the metric/dataset difference, and some claims such as matching or exceeding ground-truth-mask pose performance are phrased too strongly relative to the tables.

The ethics/impact discussion is superficial. For a robotic perception system intended to improve autonomous reliability, the paper should discuss failure modes, safety implications of false tracking confidence/relocalization, and risks under reflective/transparent objects or out-of-distribution scenes in more concrete terms.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: robust reference-conditioned 6D pose tracking without manual test-time masks, boxes, or per-instance adaptation. The combination of a learned segmentation module (SOM/HSFA) with an explicit tracking-verification module (TOM) is practically useful and targets a real failure mode of current pose trackers: silent drift under occlusion or rapid motion.

The empirical coverage is fairly broad. The paper evaluates pose estimation on LM-O and YCB-Video, segmentation over multiple BOP datasets, SAM3D reconstruction effects, tracking failure recovery, runtime, and several ablations. The reported gains over CNOS + FoundationPose and other annotation/adaptation-free segmentation baselines are substantial, especially the LM-O pose improvement and the strong BOP segmentation results.

The method is modular and likely useful to practitioners. It reuses strong frozen components and adds trainable modules for reference-query fusion and compatibility verification, which makes the approach relatively easy to integrate into existing FoundationPose-like systems. Runtime profiling is also helpful and separates initialization/re-localization costs from steady-state tracking costs.

The manuscript is mostly clear and unusually careful in places about defining its evaluation setting. In particular, it explicitly clarifies that “zero-shot” means annotation-free and adaptation-free inference, not category-disjoint novel-object generalization, and the limitations section acknowledges dependence on reference diversity, SAM3D quality, FoundationPose, and threshold calibration.

The TOM formulation is a sensible contribution. Training a binary compatibility verifier and using a smoothed energy-like score to trigger re-localization is simple, well motivated, and supported by ablations showing attention-based matching improves failure detection over cosine similarity.
weaknesses: The central “single image / no CAD” framing is not fully supported by the evaluation. SOM training uses BOP training splits and rendered views from available 3D object models, while the SAM3D pose evaluation aligns reconstructed meshes to benchmark CAD models using ICP to report under the BOP coordinate convention. The authors explain this, but it weakens the claim that the results demonstrate deployment without curated CAD assets or object-level priors.

The evidence for generalization is limited. The same benchmark object identities may appear in train and test splits, and the paper explicitly does not evaluate category-disjoint novel-object generalization. Since the proposed system is framed as reference-conditioned and annotation-free, stronger out-of-distribution object/category splits would be important before making broad claims about zero-shot physical AI deployment.

The tracking evaluation is somewhat synthetic and mild. The YCB-Video stress test uses frame dropping and random rectangular occlusions with probability 0.1, and the failure dataset is generated from synthetic identity swaps and crop perturbations. This is useful, but it does not fully establish robustness under real severe occlusion, fast camera/object motion, distractors, or multi-object tracking. The paper also claims real-world deployment motivation but does not present real robot experiments.

Some comparisons are potentially uneven or under-contextualized. Table 2 compares STORM, trained once on BOP training data plus auxiliary data, to a mixture of annotation-free leaderboard methods and supervised methods, but the exact training data, object identity overlap, and inference assumptions differ across baselines. The strong results are promising, but the fairness of the comparison is not completely transparent.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendices provide many useful hyperparameters, thresholds, data construction details, and runtime settings, but the code availability line is blank, exact architecture dimensions are not fully specified, and several baselines rely on leaderboard/executable packages. Reproducing the full pipeline, especially SAM3D reconstruction/alignment plus FoundationPose integration, would likely be difficult from the manuscript alone.

There are presentation inconsistencies that reduce confidence. For example, the text says STORM on YCB-Video “matches the ground-truth setup exactly,” while Table 1 reports 77/98/73 versus 78/99/74. The HSFA ablation AP values in Table 8 appear to be on a different scale or protocol than the main segmentation table, but this is not clearly explained. Some references and components are very recent/foundation-model dependent, increasing the need for precise versioning.

The originality is moderate rather than exceptional. HSFA is a reasonable attention-based reference-query fusion module, and TOM is an effective verifier, but much of the system performance comes from composing strong existing components such as DINOv3, CLIP/VLMs, SAM3D, and FoundationPose. The paper’s contribution is mainly system integration plus targeted learned modules, not a fundamentally new pose-estimation paradigm.
